World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Live: US fires on tankers as Tehran accuses Washington of 'reckless military adventure'
World.content:
Welcome to our live coverage of the war in the Middle East.

Overnight, the US military said it struck two empty Iranian-flagged oil tankers, which it accused of seeking to violate its ongoing blockade.

US Central Command said in a post on X that a third Iranian-flagged vessel was disabled on Wednesday.

"All three vessels are no longer transiting to Iran," it said.

Meanwhile, Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi accused the US of endangering ongoing peace talks.

World.title: Gold Coast couple ditches new build for 100-year-old home
World.content:
When Kim and Michael Kendall decided to relocate a Queenslander to the Gold Coast, they did not expect it to attract so much attention.

It was only after the 100-year-old timber home was raised and secured more than four metres above their Palm Beach block that they realised how much it stood out.

"You turn the corner and go, 'Oh God, there's a house on the block,'" Ms Kendall said.

"A lot of buildings are being pulled down in this area. There's a lot of new going up. So to see something with character come in has been quite unique."

Kim Kendall says renovating a Queenslander has been a dream come true. (ABC Gold Coast: Glenn Mullane)

The couple, who are in their 60s, said their original brick home was sinking and had to be knocked down.

Instead of building a new home, they decided to restore a traditional Queenslander, which they bought from a site in Loganholme for $190,000.

"We actually went ahead with plans for a new build, but it just wasn't sitting right with us. So we decided this is where we'd bring the Queenslander we'd always dreamed of renovating," Ms Kendall said.

"It took us six months to find it, and when we saw her, we knew this was the one."

Queenslanders are a rare sight on the Gold Coast. (Supplied: Ryer Projects)

Project 'sentimental'

Ms Kendall said the project is expected to take about two years to complete and costs more than a new build.

Despite this, she said the time and effort were worth it because of its sentimental value.

"When I was growing up in New Zealand, my grandmother had a cottage, and I spent a lot of time there, and that was some of my fondest memories as a child," she said.

" She would have been 100 this year, and her name was Shirley, and the house is 100, so it felt appropriate to call the house Shirley after her. "

The home has been named "Shirley" after Kim Kendall's grandmother. (Supplied: Ryer Projects)

Their builder, Ethan Inglis, said he was not surprised by their decision.

"They're full of character, which you can't build. And they also have an inherent energy about them as well. When you step into a Queenslander, there is a feeling associated with it, and those things, the energy, the feeling and the character, you can't build," Mr Inglis said.

"I think that's one of the things, beyond just the visual and aesthetic appeal, that attracts people to them and makes them love the homes."

Ethan Inglis says it is the first time his team have renovated a Queenslander on the Gold Coast. (ABC Gold Coast: Danielle Mahe)

Relocation 'challenging'

But he said this was the first time his team had relocated a historic home to the Gold Coast, which he admitted had been challenging.

"We have to build all the foundations before bringing it to the site, and we have to know exactly how that house measures and sits, being 100 years old," he said.

" So, it's about painting a clear picture so we can ensure it comes out of the ground correctly, because that's the part you have to get perfect for the job to flow well. "

Relocating the Queenslander was complex. (Supplied: Ryer Projects)

Heritage expert Benjamin Gall said that while renovating and relocating Queenslanders is not new, it was uncommon to see one relocated to the southern Gold Coast.

"Historically, Palm Beach consisted of beach places and shacks," Mr Gall said.

"If you go over the border into New South Wales, timber-and-tin homes are certainly more common there than they are on the Gold Coast."

Mr Gall said projects like this are beneficial and sustainable for the environment, and he commended the Kendalls for preserving a historic building.

"It's a courageous thing to take on at the Gold Coast. I'm sure they'll attract a great amount of attention, and I look forward to seeing the finished product."

World.title: Trump releases UFO files in 'unprecedented transparency'
World.content:
US President Donald Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth have released dozens of previously classified files on alleged UFO sightings and alien life to provide what they call "unprecedented transparency" to the American people.

The disclosure of the long-sought documents and photos of "unidentified anomalous phenomena" (UAP) will be followed by future releases as more materials are declassified, the US Defense Department said in a statement.

Mr Trump is the latest US president to release reports on UFOs that date back to the 1940s and were first disclosed in the late 1970s.

Experts said the batch of about 160 files released on Friday contained new videos of known sightings but gave no conclusive evidence of extraterrestrial life.

A football-shaped object, reported by the US Indo-Pacific Command in 2024, was among the images released. (Supplied: Department of Defense via Reuters )

The files include a 1947 report of "flying discs" as well as a photo of "unidentified phenomena" taken from the Moon's surface during the Apollo 12 lunar mission in 1969.

Images of 'bright particles' and mystery objects

It also included a transcript of the Apollo 17 crew describing unidentified objects seen from the Moon in 1972.

Apollo 17 mission pilot Ronald Evans reported "a few very bright particles or fragments or something that go drifting by as we manoeuvrer," based on the transcript.

"Roger. Understand," mission control replied.

"These files, hidden behind classifications, have long fuelled justified speculation — and it's time the American people see it for themselves," Mr Hegseth said in a statement.

The records release is likely to fuel fresh debate over government secrecy and the possible existence of life in the cosmos.

"Whereas previous Administrations have failed to be transparent on this subject, with these new Documents and Videos, the people can decide for themselves, "WHAT THE HELL IS GOING ON?" Mr Trump said in a statement.

"Have fun and enjoy!"

US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth summoned senior military leaders from around the world for the meeting. (Reuters: Jonathan Ernst)

The move was welcomed by US Representatives Tim Burchett and Anna Paulina Luna, both proponents of declassifying UFO files.

Ms Luna said an additional tranche of material was expected in about 30 days.

"The files show that UAP are not simply a matter of speculation or public curiosity," Harvard University astrophysicist Avi Loeb said.

"The government has collected records."

The images from Apollo 12 and 17 were fascinating but could be the result of asteroid impacts on the lunar surface, Mr Loeb said. He added that more interesting material was likely still to come, but would take longer to declassify.

Distraction from political problems?

Donald Trump's name appears 38,000 times in the Epstein files, according to the Department of Justice records. (AP Photo: Jon Elswick)

Some critics cast the UFO disclosures as a distraction from Mr Trump's political woes, including the unpopular US military campaign against Iran and public pressure to release further files tied to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

"I really don't care about the UFO files. I just don't. I'm so sick of the 'look at the shiny object' propaganda," former Republican US representative Marjorie Taylor Greene wrote on X.

UFO sighting mystery lingers In 1966, more than a hundred school children witnessed UFOs hovering overhead. Today they are marking the 60th anniversary and demanding an explanation because "they know what they saw".

Ms Greene, once a strong supporter of the US president and leader within the MAGA movement, has fallen out with Mr Trump.

UAP investigator Mick West said the administration of former president Joe Biden disclosed much of the same information as Friday's release. Mr West, who produces software to analyse UAP videos, said the files provided no new evidence on the possible existence of alien life.

"They're evidence of us not being able to identify a small white dot that's a long distance away," said the Sacramento, California-based analyst, adding that shapes in UAP videos were often camera lens diffraction from bright light.

Independent journalist Leslie Kean said the release showed there was still a lot of government information on UAP that should be disclosed.

Ms Kean co-authored a 2017 New York Times story on a secret Pentagon UAP program, which prompted Congress to push for declassification of UFO documents.

"I think we've already proven the existence of UAP, but that doesn't mean we've proven they're alien or extraterrestrial or that we know what they are," Ms Kean said.

Reuters/ABC

World.title: Tasmania rejected an on‑country hearing but other courts show how it works
World.content:
A Tasmanian court's rejection of a request to hold a hearing on Aboriginal-owned land has been described by an Indigenous anti-logging protester as a "missed opportunity".

Yorta Yorta/Dja Dja Wurrung woman Ruth Langford, who is also known as Tipruthanna, made the offer at the end of March while representing herself in the Hobart Magistrates Court.

She is facing a charge of trespass after she protested against native forest logging at Snow Hill in the northern midlands in 2025.

She applied to the court to have her hearing take place at Piyura Kitina/Risdon Cove on Hobart's eastern shore — the first British settlement site in the area and the location of a colonial massacre of Aboriginal people in Tasmania.

The request was for the hearing to take place at the Aboriginal Community Centre at Piyura Kitina/Risdon Cove. (ABC News)

In making her decision, Magistrate Catherine Geason said there may be an appropriate future case for an on-country hearing in Tasmania, but the matter in question could be fairly and properly assessed in a regular court.

But while the idea has been rejected in Tasmania, for now, other states and territories have shown how an on-country hearing or greater involvement of Indigenous legal principles can happen.

What is an on-country hearing?

An on-country hearing is where court proceedings are held on Aboriginal land or land relevant to the legal matter, allowing for evidence to be heard in the context of cultural obligations to land and waters, and in a more culturally safe setting.

"Our identity and cultural knowledge can be best and most reliably heard when we are connected to our country," Ms Langford/Tipruthanna said to those outside court on the day of the hearing.

The Tasmanian Aboriginal Centre's Nala Mansell (left) and Ruth Langford (right) outside court. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

In the Northern Territory, two on-country hearings were held during a landmark case concerning the destruction of a sacred site at the Kakadu National Park.

In 2023, the Federal Court also travelled to the Torres Strait Islands for a climate case involving traditional owners of Boigu and Saibai islands, who failed in their attempt to sue the Commonwealth for failing to protect their homelands from climate change, but are now appealing against the decision.

Lawyers in traditional robes at the Federal Court sitting at Noonkanbah Station, which determined in favour of Native Title claimants. (ABC Kimberley: Ben Collins)

Other matters regarding native title have also been heard on country, including a "history-making" case at the Noonkanbah cattle station in the Kimberly in 2007.

How other jurisdictions recognise Indigenous practices

Interstate and overseas jurisdictions, including the United States, Canada, South Africa, and New Zealand, have established court systems that recognise both Indigenous and colonial practices.

For example, the Rangatahi and Pasifika courts in New Zealand operate under the same laws as the Youth Court but take place on marae (at Māori meeting sites) or Pasifika churches, but follow Māori or Pasifika cultural practices.

A session of Rangatahi Court in New Zealand. (Supplied: District Court of New Zealand)

Canada now has at least 19 Gladue courts that do not follow alternative laws to mainstream courts but recognise the backgrounds of an accused Indigenous person by drawing on community knowledge holders.

The first Gladue Court opened in 2001 in Toronto after the Canadian Supreme Court acknowledged the role of colonialism in over-incarceration of Indigenous people and decided that this should be considered in conventional legal systems.

Similarly in Australia, Victoria now has around 17 'Koori' courts, which aim to improve outcomes for Aboriginal people who plead guilty, while New South Wales has multiple Youth Koori Courts.

A Welcome to Country dance being performed at the opening of the Youth Koori Court in Dubbo, NSW.

Koori courts operate under the same state laws as mainstream courts, but allow Aboriginal elders to sit around the table with the magistrate and defendant, along with other relevant people such as lawyers, a corrections staff member, or a court officer.

A Victorian pilot program also provided Aboriginal Community Justice Reports (ACJR), which aimed to acknowledge the role of a person's disadvantage, including through intergenerational impacts of colonisation, in offending.

The pilot, which ended in 2025, was seen as "a circuit breaker to high and rising incarceration rates in Victoria" in an evaluation by the University of Technology Sydney.

Indigenous people are going to jail at a record rate — what's the solution? The number of Indigenous people behind bars is rising. But some judges are bucking the trend by taking a different approach.

The in-depth reports are gathered alongside a person and provided to courts, detailing their life history, Aboriginal and social factors, impacts of colonisation and "attitudes towards past actions and future plans".

But the director of the program, the Victorian Aboriginal Legal Service's Marie Mitchell, said the reports allowed people to reflect in a way that was absent in mainstream courts.

"They're incredibly in-depth reports going through a person's history, impacts of intergenerational trauma, the colonial history in terms of their mob and their family," Ms Mitchell said.

Marie Mitchell says the reports provided to the court detail not only the offender's history but intergenerational impacts such as the effect of colonisations. (Supplied: Victorian Aboriginal Legal Service)

"Really sort of weaving that into what's led them to be sitting before the court on that day, and that person might have some reflections on where they'd like to go to, from that day.

"Often these children, now adults, have been the people who have fallen through those gaps."

But Ms Mitchell said Victorian programs were not perfect, saying more pre-resolution initiatives were needed.

Victoria is the only Australian state or territory with improved rates of adult Indigenous incarceration in 2025.

Why do some think it is important?

Advocates and Aboriginal community members say current legal systems implemented by Western institutions do not fit long-standing Aboriginal principles that were uprooted on arrival by colonial settlers.

"When the white people invaded Aboriginal lands, they set up their own legal system completely based on the needs and values of white people," the Tasmanian Aboriginal Centre's Nala Mansell said.

Ms Mansell says courts have not been set up for the needs and cultural values of First Nations people. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

With Aboriginal people increasingly over-represented in Australian prisons and courts, advocates believe that incorporating Indigenous principles into the justice system is one way forward.

Despite Closing the Gap targets to reduce Indigenous imprisonment, Tasmania is going backwards, a position that reflects the nation's overall statistics.

About 5 per cent of Tasmanians identify as Aboriginal, but Aboriginal people make up 44 per cent of Tasmania's prison population — according to statistics from March this year — an increase of 6 per cent from the previous year.

"The benefit of having a court process such as [those interstate that] supports cultural safety; that understanding of identity, the history and the colonialism that sits around it, and of the colonial framework that sits in the mainstream court system," Aboriginal Legal Service chief executive Jake Smith said.

Jake Smith says Tasmania's Aboriginal community doesn't have access to a culturally appropriate pathway through the legal system. (ABC News)

Mr Smith said a pilot of a bail support program ensuring an accused person was connected with an Aboriginal community member had "shown really strong outcomes" for reducing recidivism.

"One of the successful components of that was that support through a service that understands how the community operates, the experiences of the Aboriginal community, and how to connect people through the different services that are culturally appropriate," Mr Smith said.

Federal Court hears landmark early testimony from WA elders Five Karajarri elders have testified before the Federal Court in anticipation of a compensation claim set to be lodged in 2026.

But Mr Smith said more investment was needed for early intervention programs for both youths and adults.

"The earlier we can support mob, our people, the greater outcomes we will have around reducing over-representation," he said.

The state government said reducing the number of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in the corrections system was one of the key priorities of its 'Changing Lives, Creating Futures' strategic plan, which it released in 2023.

It said it was committed to improving access to justice for all Tasmanians.

"The Tasmanian government has no plans to make legislative amendments to allow cases to be heard on country," a spokesperson said.

World.title: Investigators head to Geraldton as dust fears rise with iron ore expansion
World.content:
Fears Geraldton could turn into "the next Port Hedland" are intensifying as dust from iron ore operations blankets homes and businesses in parts of the coastal city.

Dean Parker says his workplace is constantly covered in black dust. (ABC Midwest Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Residents have raised concerns about health, property damage and the long-term impact of expanding mining in Western Australia's Midwest.

Investigators from the Department of Water and Environmental Regulation (DWER) visited Geraldton last week after a surge in dust-related complaints.

There are calls for the trains to be fully covered to help stop the spread of iron ore dust. (ABC Midwest Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

The agency has launched two investigations and will assess the characteristics of the dust and its likely sources.

Dust on the wind

Residents and businesses are reporting a noticeable increase in dust around their properties. (ABC Midwest Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Geraldton's port sits beside the CBD, with rail lines and roads carrying iron ore looping past suburbs, schools and the hospital.

Two major exporters dominate the trade: Chinese‑owned Karara Mining, which ships magnetite concentrate, and WA‑based Fenix Resources, which exports hematite.

Iron ore trains travel about 250km to Geraldton Port with their carriages uncovered. (ABC Midwest Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Their transport methods differ sharply. Fenix uses covered quad road trains, while Karara hauls ore in uncovered rail wagons.

In a region known for strong southerly summer winds, locals say dust is impossible to ignore.

Costing money

Some of the dust Dean Parker has gathered from his gutters at Fishermen's Wharf, situated next to the Geraldton Port. (ABC Midwest Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Marine service provider Dean Parker regularly sweeps magnetic black dust from his workshop gutters at the Geraldton Fishermen's Harbour, which he believes is magnetite.

"You can run a magnet through the gutters and it just sticks to it," he said.

" It gets into the paint, into the nooks and crannies, it starts the corrosion process. "

Dean Parker wants the iron ore trains to be covered. (ABC Midwest Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

He said dust could also be found along railway tracks leading into the port and was damaging sheds, boats and infrastructure.

"It feels like they're just vandalising our town and not caring," he said.

Crayfisher Peter Bailey said the problem had become worse in the past year, and he was watching his shed rust away.

Peter Bailey has become increasingly frustrated with the dust covering his boat. (ABC Midwest Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

"Everything seems to be covered in black dust," he said.

"We can come in at five in the afternoon, wash the boats, and leave early the next morning, and the boats are covered in dust."

Mr Bailey said there was a marked difference between normal "dirt-based" dust and what was sticking to his boat, which was difficult to remove.

Peter Bailey says he has to resurface his boat sooner due to the black dust. (ABC Midwest Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

He was spending $25,000 resurfacing one of his boats — work he would normally do every five or six years but was now forced to do after just two.

"It's frustrating because someone is responsible here," he said.

Fishers are washing the dust from their boats to try to reduce corrosion. (ABC Midwest Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

What's in the dust?

Beachlands resident Anna Kolosinska said her home had become increasingly coated in black dust or "soot" over the past five years, which she believed was blowing from the rail line used by Karara.

Anna Kolosinska says dust coats her home and car despite regular cleaning. (ABC Midwest Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

"It's got really bad, I'm cleaning once a week quite heavily," she said.

"I'm noticing the floors especially having dust build up and on the windows as well as outside.

"I could wash my car, or it could rain, and the following day it's covered in dust."

Geraldton Port is located within the town centre, in close proximity to residential areas. (ABC Midwest Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Beachlands local Ralf Mulks scraped dust from his exterior wall and sent it for laboratory analysis.

"The results came back showing 28 per cent magnetite," he said.

Mr Mulks has led a campaign encouraging the community to formally lodge dust complaints to DWER.

Ralf Mulks has commissioned independent dust testing to better understand what it contains. (ABC Midwest Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Particle size is key

Respiratory physician Scott Claxton said particle size was important when assessing health risks.

"The larger the particle, the less distance it can get down into your airway," he said.

Scott Claxton says more research is needed into the long-term health impacts of exposure to airborne particles. (ABC Midwest Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

But he said substances in dust could still be absorbed into the body as they dissolve in the respiratory system.

"It's similar to if you swallowed it, you'll absorb it, if you breathe it in, you can absorb it as well," he said.

He said more research was needed on long-term exposure to airborne particles near industrial areas.

But Dr Claxton said grain dust was more likely to cause immediate respiratory irritation.

Between 2 and 3 million tonnes of grain is exported from Geraldton annually.

Last year, Mid West Port handled a record 19.1 million tonnes of cargo, mostly iron ore. (ABC Midwest Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

A growing port

In the past 15 years, throughput at the Geraldton Port has roughly doubled to 19.1 million tonnes, driven largely by iron ore.

DWER investigators will examine the dust and trace its sources. (ABC Midwest Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Long-term growth plans could eventually see capacity expand to as much as 50 million tonnes per year.

Former mayor Shane Van Styn, who lives 400 metres from the port, said the scale of growth raised serious questions.

"No-one's contemplated this volume of iron ore and dust coming into a port located this close to a town site," he said.

Shane Van Styn supports mining and iron ore exports but says Mid West Ports should share more information with the community. (ABC Midwest Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

" We need to demonstrate our credentials as being a leading port city that can do its work without polluting its people and creating the next Port Hedland. "

Port Hedland exports more than 500 million tonnes of iron ore each year.

Hundreds of homes near its port have been surrendered under a voluntary buyback scheme due to dust pollution.

The 13.5 million tonnes exported through Geraldton last year is small by comparison, but the Midwest industry is steadily expanding.

Fenix Resources aims to lift annual exports from 4.5 million tonnes to 10 million tonnes, while Karara Mining has long-term plans to remain in the region and operates infrastructure capable of handling up to 16 million tonnes annually.

Mid West Port uses a netting designed to help contain dust but strong summer winds can weaken and degrade it over time. (ABC Midwest Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

1970s-style transport

The rail line and road access to the port loop through residential suburbs and past facilities such as schools and hospitals. (ABC Midwest Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

City of Greater Geraldton Mayor Jerry Clune said coexistence between exporters and residents was possible, but improvements were needed.

"We've got to balance the economic benefit it has to our community on top of the livability of a town," he said.

"There's some users of the port that are very good with the control of their dust, and then there's others that probably leave a little bit to be desired; it's back to the 1970s style of how they transport their product."

Jerry Clune says the council is advocating for increased dust monitoring across the community. (ABC Midwest Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Mr Clune said he had personally witnessed dust blowing from loaded trains.

"On the roads, if you're not covered, you'll be pinged for an unsecured load," he said.

Mid West Ports says it is working with the department investigating dust associated with rail freight operations. (ABC Midwest Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

He supports more dust monitoring outside the port and greater transparency about the dust contents.

Mid West Ports declined an interview but said it was monitoring dust, and had invested in dust‑mitigation projects, including a dust‑tamer fence, and that dust exceedence incidents had decreased.

"DWER is currently investigating dust associated with rail freight operations, with Mid West Ports supporting this work," the statement said.

Karara transports black magnetite ore in uncovered rail wagons. (ABC Midwest Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

The port said it operated under strict environmental licence conditions.

The ABC requested interviews with the minister for environment and Karara Mining; the minister declined and Karara did not respond.

Kirrilee Warr has asked questions in parliament about Geraldton's dust pollution. (ABC Midwest Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Member for Geraldton Kirrilee Warr said the community was frustrated by the silence of government.

"We are hearing from everyone … even further inland throughout more agricultural areas around dust coming from moving trains," the Nationals MP said.

Mid West Ports declined an interview request, but said in a statement it had invested in dust mitigation. (ABC Midwest Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Other users

Fenix Resources executive chair John Welborn said the company was upgrading its port facilities to reduce dust as it expanded, and if the company moved to rail, it would use covered wagons.

Two of its wharf sheds are connected to a covered conveyor system, but the remaining shed is not, and he acknowledged it could generate dust and road staining.

John Welborn is the head of Fenix Resources, which is upgrading its facilities at the port. (ABC Midwest Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

"The only way we can get iron ore into that shed currently is by driving the trucks into the shed and side tipping onto the floor of the shed," he said.

"That is a very dusty activity … dust can escape from that shed, but also the truck has to drive on top of the material that it's just unloaded."

Mr Welborn said Fenix would spend $8 million this year connecting the remaining shed to the covered conveyor system, which would "see a huge improvement".

Fenix currently transports all of its iron ore to port by truck but plans to use covered trains as it expands. (ABC Midwest Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

He said dust during ship loading was the port's responsibility and not a major issue.

On concerns about the health impact of inhaling iron ore dust, Mr Welborn said Fenix products were rigorously tested as part of its export licence.

Ralf Mulks is leading a campaign encouraging residents to complain about the dust to the DWER. (ABC Midwest Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

"Particularly in the Pilbara, there's been an enormous amount of work done on iron oxide, which is effectively the dust that's created by iron ore," he said.

"There has been no causal link established between iron oxide and negative health impacts."

Watch ABC TV's Landline at 12:30pm AEST on Sunday or stream anytime on ABC iview.

There are concerns about what may be entering nearby waterways, as fishers wash their boats at the wharf daily. (ABC Midwest Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

World.title: Julie Bishop was adamant she wasn't going anywhere — until she did
World.content:
Julie Bishop, as so often has been her way, was resolute.

Unmoved.

When the vice-chancellor she served alongside at the Australian National University (ANU) resigned in September last year, then-chancellor Bishop was unequivocal — she wasn't going anywhere.

"There are no grounds for me to stand aside," she told a packed media conference at the time.

"I have the backing of council, and I intend to see it through."

Until she didn't.

December 31 was the date when Ms Bishop was due to finish her term, so the obvious question is why — having repeatedly stated she would see her commitment through — did she leave months earlier? And did she jump, or was she pushed?

Julie Bishop was due to finish her term as the chancellor of the Australian National Univerity on December 31 this year. (ABC News: David Sciasci)

For her part, in a public statement announcing her resignation, Ms Bishop said that she continued to "regard the ANU as a truly national treasure".

She also noted concerns with university governance across the country, saying the higher education sector was "at a crossroads of regulatory overreach in the governance of our institutions or autonomy and academic freedom".

"I fear the collateral from this regulatory overreach will be the next generation of students and staff," she said.

Do you know more? Contact Adam Shirley on encrypted email. Please note end-to-end encryption is only possible with your own encrypted email system like Protonmail.

A high-profile office holder will always have staunch supporters, opponents, and many others in between.

But some clues as to why further upheaval has beset an already teetering institution are staring students, staff and the taxpaying public right in the face.

Julie Bishop oversaw the ANU during a tumultuous period. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Multiple investigations underway

There are currently six (count them) investigations involving the ANU — if you include the implementation phase of the review into alleged "wildly inappropriate behaviour" at the College of Health and Medicine.

One of those investigations has just been completed — an independent review about former Australian National University council members, which found five adverse findings against them.

A draft report into the reasoning and management of the now-aborted $250 million savings plan called 'Renew ANU' has also found the cost-cutting was approved without clear evidence it was needed or achievable.

And a highly anticipated release is the university regulator, Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency (TEQSA), inquiry into the ANU Council's decisions, leadership and internal culture, which some, including ACT independent senator David Pocock, want released as soon as practically possible.

ACT Senator David Pocock is among those calling for the TEQSA inquiry to be released as soon as possible. (ABC News: Luke Stephenson)

All the investigations are assessing various forms of alleged poor conduct at an institution that is supposed to be revered worldwide. The alleged behaviours range from bullying, harassment, mistreatment, governance issues, financial mismanagement to possible freedom of information breaches by the ANU.

These reviews have all occurred during Ms Bishop's six-year tenure as chancellor.

While it's premature to conclude there is any direct link between these facts, the pressure on Ms Bishop as the institution's figurehead during this time — and the associated reputational damage to the ANU — is significant.

More resignations to come?

Beyond reputations, though, the real-world collateral hits hardest.

Whether it is students missing out on courses they were dedicated to, staff being dismissed or left in the lurch about their futures, or allegations of significant trauma meted out to people within the ANU's wall, lives have been harmed and livelihoods have been permanently scarred.

This may not be the end of the resignations from senior ranks of the ANU. Some are calling on appointed members of the ANU Council to seriously consider whether they should follow Ms Bishop's lead and head for the exits.

Until a replacement chancellor is found, the man warming the seat is current pro-chancellor Dr Larry Marshall — himself no stranger to controversy and staff disquiet during his years leading the CSIRO.

But amid the turbulence at the ANU, staff and students still profess a genuine love for a place where they learn, work and strive to do their best.

They will be hoping that these painful public losses will lead to more harmonious and productive days ahead.

World.title: Former ACT politician allegedly groomed teen with dinners, alcohol
World.content:
New details have emerged about how former ACT attorney-general Gordon Ramsay is alleged to have groomed a boy with dinners, alcohol and by telling him he was special, before requesting increasingly sexualised images.

Mr Ramsay was arrested in October last year after a complaint to police, when he was charged with grooming the teen between 2022 and 2024.

Until now, the ACT Magistrates Court had suppressed court documents containing details about the alleged offence, on which the charge is based.

But after an application by the ABC to lift the suppression, Magistrate Jane Campbell ordered a redacted version of the document be made public.

Communication began on Instagram

The documents reveal allegations the pair began communicating on Instagram, and would catch up for dinner at least once a week, often at expensive steak houses, followed by the theatre.

Their meetings are said to have included weekend catch-ups and phone calls.

"The defendant began messaging … 'Good morning' and 'Good night' every day along with lengthy messages throughout the day," the statement of facts alleges.

" In a single day [the alleged victim] would receive more messages from the defendant than the rest of his friends combined. "

Police say after a few months, Mr Ramsay is alleged to have told the boy he "was very special".

He is also alleged to have said: "he would treat him as an adult and would keep the communication between only them".

The statement of facts also suggests that Mr Ramsay knew the teen's family had a strict 'no alcohol before 18' policy, but gave him small bottles anyway.

'Continually suggested more sexualised content'

The police statement of facts alleges Mr Ramsay then began suggesting the boy send him photos he referred to as SPUN images, which related to the removal of clothing.

"The defendant created an online shared folder on iCloud ... only accessible by the pair … to upload the SPUN images to," the statement of facts alleges.

"The SPUN images were to be taken by [the alleged victim] and uploaded daily.

"The SPUN images started out as photos of [the alleged victim] posing smiling and clothed."

The documents allege Mr Ramsay later suggested the boy take photos of himself in his underwear.

"[The boy] … was initially hesitant to do this, however the defendant reassured him, stating that if he has trusted everything until now, that he could keep trusting him," the statement of facts alleges.

"The defendant continually pushed … boundaries with the SPUN photographs and continually suggested more sexualised content."

Arrest following search of car, home

It is alleged that Mr Ramsay had also been buying the boy clothes, including underwear and later lingerie.

It is also alleged he purchased numerous sex toys as gifts.

The police statement notes concern raised by the boy's family in June 2024 about how much time the pair were spending together.

Later in the year, Mr Ramsay is alleged to have messaged the boy saying due to his "parents mentioning going to the police, they needed to delete the SPUN photographs".

Mr Ramsay is then alleged to have sent an email saying all the photos would be in one folder on his device and he would delete the shared folder and the boy should do the same.

Mr Ramsay was arrested after searches of his car and home, when several electronic devices alleged to contain the messages between the pair were seized.

He has pleaded not guilty, but the case has dragged after prosecutors and police said the forensic examination of his devices was taking some time.

Mr Ramsay will be back in court later in the month.

Material released without appropriate redactions

As well as being ordered to release the court documents, the Magistrates Court has also been asked to consider the conduct of the Office of the ACT Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP), after a copy of the material was sent to the ABC without appropriate redactions.

The court heard correspondence between the ABC and the DPP's office as the challenge to the suppressions was being put together, revealed the breach, which happened while the court prohibition was still in place.

The ABC said it erased the material soon afterwards.

Magistrate Campbell said given the document was in breach of the court order revealing suppressed material, the court should look at whether the incident should be referred to the police.

But she said she had stopped short of any reference to contempt of court.

World.title: The Devil Wears Prada 2 is a tepid re-heat of the original
World.content:
How it breaks my heart to say it, but the fashion isn't as good.

The women aren't as funny. The boyfriends aren't as villainous.

And what has happened to the unsmiling, highly critical and exceptionally competent woman who is the Devil herself? As befits these times of trad wives and shrinking women's rights, she's had a few fangs removed, too.

Fans are swooning to have the band of Meryl Streep, Anne Hathaway, Emily Blunt and Stanley Tucci back together in the much-hyped sequel to the 2006 smash, The Devil Wears Prada, and in these dark and uncertain times, a little Dior goes a long way.

But, friends, and I do hate to say it, TDWP2 is like so many of these delayed reboots: a shadow of its size six past. And when you are paying good money in tight times to see the sequel to the most fashionable and adored romantic comedy of modern times… that's a tough trifecta.

And be warned, there are spoilers galore here.

Miranda Priestly has lost her fangs in the reboot as weak plot lines make room for superfluous scenes and characters.

A tepid re-heat of the original

After hearing Meryl Streep wax on about how the team finally created a script that justified a sequel, I was profoundly shocked at the banality of the dialogue, the simple shot-for-shot remakes, and that maddeningly slow pace that seems to affect all rom-coms these days.

The film is a tepid re-heat of old character clashes and foibles that decades of work experience seem to have left unaffected. The movie attempts a story context of dying legacy media, but that can serve as little more than a taster, when no superhero can come along and save the day for colour mags — not even the Emilys.

But, by all means, explain this glacial pace!

You've seen it yourself, I'm sure, in the new generation of rom-coms rolling through. The contrast was powerful between the original episodes of Sex and the City and its sequel, And Just Like That, with crackling dialogue replaced by ponderous pace and flat language.



In Prada, reaction times and the words that go with them have been slowed, and the effect is to sap energy from the film. The divine Tucci, whose Nigel was the sparkling seltzer in any scene, appears to be mildly sedated.

There are superfluous scenes and superfluous characters (Patrick Brammall is a delight; he's funny just by being there, but his character is completely unnecessary and simply slows things down) and in the end it's very hard to understand why the filmmakers thought this whole go-round was necessary.

There's a theory going around that explains some of this: streaming platform insiders have suggested over the years that they deliberately write and edit their content to account for our distraction.

They know that we are double-screening while we watch most shows, so they make dialogue very exposition-heavy, with large flag posts about where the story is going, and they extend reaction and response times within dialogue, so we don't miss too much plot advancement while our heads are buried in our phones.

Try it yourself: play an old episode of say, The West Wing or Moonlighting, and see if you can keep up after your hand has idly reached for your phone. The easier contrast is with the original TDWP: it's 10 minutes shorter and at least 15 degrees sharper than the new one.

The disappointment I felt watching the new movie was profound. TDWP1 was a rare and charming thing. It was a rom-com where the true love interest is between women — for fashion and for each other's success — but it's still one that many men love just as much.

I'm fond of Emily Blunt's anecdote about her husband John Krazinski's affection for the original's famous sequence of Andrea's fabulous multiple work looks, which he watches closely until "….. aaaaaand THAT's my favourite".

But what do I know? The Devil Wears Prada 2 smashed its opening weekend, earning $234 million globally, and nearly tripling the original's opening take in 2006.

The first film was a rom-com where the true love interest is between women — for fashion and for each other's success. (Supplied: 20th Century Studios)

'Don't you just love it?'

One small, but shining moment towards the end of the film represents a missed opportunity to make a sequel that lives up to its promise. After a key win, Miranda turns to Andrea and, in a bookend to her now well-memed observation of "everybody wants this", she smiles with deep pleasure and says: "I love working so much. Don't you just love it?"

Her happy observation arrives just shy of 40 years after working women like Diane Keaton in Baby Boom were brought to heel by babies and suburbia; or humiliated and downgraded like Sigourney Weaver in Working Girl or Demi Moore in Disclosure; or literally shot through the heart for refusing to play the silent girlfriend like Glenn Close in Fatal Attraction.

In movies, it remains a novel idea that an ambitious, successful woman should still be happy with all that by the time the credits roll; not even Katherine Hepburn or Rosalind Russell got away with that free of the chains of marriage at the zenith of their screwball comedies.

Miranda's joy at her working life is a tonic at a time when trad wives and crunchy mums are having a moment due to the double-whammy of powerfully misogynistic social media and a US administration determined to roll back women's rights. The attractiveness of this notion marries nicely with the "competency porn" theory making the rounds to explain why shows like The Pitt and the recent moon flight have captured imaginations: people are craving ability and excellence at a time of political stupidity.

Was Sigourney Weaver, as Ripley of the Alien franchise, the last female film character we allowed to be unsmiling, highly critical, singularly competent, impatient and above all correct? As the internet says, they should have listened to the single woman with that cat.

Miranda ends the new TDWP2 as the greatest fashion editor of her times, and she seems to live happily ever after, alongside her equally happy — and competent — colleague Andrea, and that makes these women's storylines a fairytale for the ages.

This weekend, get informed about how even the humble pub is being corporatised, even while communities try to claw these spaces back, and away from pokies, for some real social connection.

Have a safe and happy weekend. I'm happy to report that that the now immortal TDWP1 song is still a banger. Go well.

Virginia Trioli is presenter of Creative Types and a former co-host of ABC News Breakfast and Mornings on ABC Radio Melbourne.

World.title: Labor announces $40 million boost to address firearms registry failings
World.content:
The government will inject nearly $40 million into the state’s firearm registry in a bid to overhaul the troubled system and increase community safety following the Bondi shooting terror attack in December last year.

On Saturday, police minister Yasmin Catley announced the $39.3 million investment, which will also fund additional staff and system upgrades, to accompany a suite of tighter restrictions on gun owners.

Police Minister Yasmin Catley, who had described the NSW Firearms Registry as a “shambles”, and Premier Chris Minns. Dominic Lorrimer

The new restrictions reduce the licence period from five years to two, strengthen checks on people seeking to own firearms and cap the number of firearms a person can own. A comprehensive audit of all existing firearm licences will also be undertaken.

It follows a report in this masthead revealing that, during a meeting at police headquarters on December 8, 2020, psychologist and gun club official Daniel Gregg warned officials from the NSW Police Firearms Registry that far too little was being done to encourage club members to spot and report any signs of extremism among their fellow shooters.

World.title: Russia, Ukraine agree to three-day ceasefire, says Trump
World.content:
Updated WorldEuropeRussia-Ukraine war Russia, Ukraine agree to three-day ceasefire, says Trump Updated May 9, 2026 — 7:30am ,first published 4:36am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

US President Donald Trump said there will be a three-day ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine over the weekend, as well as a prisoner swap. The ceasefire, which Trump said would run from May 9 to May 11, coincides with Russia’s Victory Day celebrations, the US president said in a social media post on Friday. US President Donald Trump during a Mother’s Day luncheon at the White House on Friday. Bloomberg Trump said that Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky have both agreed to the proposal. “This Ceasefire will include a suspension of all kinetic activity, and also a prison swap of 1,000 prisoners from each Country,” Trump wrote. “Hopefully, it is the beginning of the end of a very long, deadly, and hard fought War,” he wrote on Truth Social.



Trump’s announcement also said each country, locked in more than four years of conflict, would be exchanging 1000 prisoners of war. Related Article Trump diplomacy ‘Disintegration’: Trump angers Europe with tariffs and troop withdrawal Both Kyiv and Moscow have accused the other of violating ceasefires declared separately this week as Russia readies to hold a Victory Day parade on May 9 that marks the 1945 Soviet victory over Nazi Germany. Trump has grown increasingly frustrated by the lack of progress in ending the Ukraine-Russia war, and a halt in fighting offers a bit of good news for the US president, whose war against Iran with Israel has hurt his domestic approval rating. Efforts to end the Iran war, now in its third month, appeared stalled amid new flare-ups in fighting in the Gulf. Zelensky, writing on Telegram, confirmed the ceasefire had been arranged as part of US negotiating efforts and that humanitarian issues remained a key priority.



“That is why today, within the framework of the negotiation process mediated by the American side, we received Russia’s agreement to conduct a prisoner of war exchange in the format of 1000 for 1000,” Zelensky wrote. Zelensky also issued a tongue-in-cheek decree “allowing” Russia’s May 9 military parade to proceed and saying Ukrainian weapons would not target Red Square. Officials said on Thursday that Ukraine’s top ​negotiator, Rustem Umerov, had arrived in Miami for a series of meetings with US ‌representatives as peace talks on ending Russia’s war in Ukraine have stalled in recent months. The US-brokered talks ⁠are deadlocked over Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region. Moscow demands Kyiv pull troops back from parts ​of the region it has failed to capture in its four-year full-scale invasion. Ukraine says it ​will not cede land that it controls. Moscow and Kyiv have both accused each other of violating ceasefires that each has separately declared.

World.title: Pentagon begins releasing decades of files on UFOs, unexplained phenomena
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaTrump's White House Pentagon begins releasing decades of files on UFOs, unexplained phenomena Michael Koziol May 9, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: The Pentagon has started releasing what it says are “never-before-seen files” related to reports of unidentified flying objects (UFOs), including videos and photographs of phenomena captured from US military posts around the world. Many of the images published on Friday (US time) are murky black-and-white photos or video clips in which the purported flying object is unclear and resembles only a dot or black circle. Loading Others, however, show a more defined object. One brief clip taken from a US military infrared sensor in the East China Sea in 2024 purports to show a “football-shaped body” in motion. Another, taken from a censor in the Middle East in 2013, purportedly depicts “an area of contrast resembling an eight-pointed star with arms of alternating length”.



A note accompanying each clip declares that the description provided is for “informational purposes only” and readers should not interpret it as an analytical judgment, investigative conclusion, or factual determination. The Pentagon said the area of contrast “resembles a football-shaped body with three radial projections”. US Department of War Several images appeared to relate to the same purported sighting. The trove also contains declassified witness reports about object sightings going back to the 1940s. One recent report detailed an incident in which three separate teams of federal special agents purported to witness Orange “orbs” in the sky that emitted or launched smaller red “orbs” in groups of two to four, then disappear. These events were purportedly witnessed in the western US by multiple teams at various vantage points over the course of two days in 2023.



Another showed a site photo with a rendered graphic overlay which the Pentagon said depicted “corroborating eyewitness reports from September 2023 of an apparent ellipsoid bronze metallic object materialising out of a bright light in the sky”, which had disappeared “instantaneously”. The rendered graphic overlay of reports in September 2023. US Department of War The Pentagon – which last year imposed requirements on journalists that a court found were unconstitutional – said the files’ release was part of the Trump administration’s commitment to “unprecedented transparency” regarding Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena - a modern term for UFOs. Defence Secretary Pete Hegeth said keeping the records classified had long fuelled “justified speculation” by the public, and it was time the American people saw the material for themselves. Additional files would be released on a rolling basis “as they are discovered and declassified”, the Pentagon said, with new tranches expected every few weeks.



US President Donald Trump urged people to draw their own conclusions about what they could see in the files. “In an effort for Complete and Maximum Transparency, it was my Honor to direct my Administration to identify and provide Government files related to Alien and Extraterrestrial Life, Unidentified Aerial Phenomena, and Unidentified Flying Objects,” Trump said on Truth Social. Related Article Exclusive

Space Want to visit space after Artemis II? For $20m, Anousheh flew herself there “Whereas previous Administrations have failed to be transparent on this subject, with these new Documents and Videos, the people can decide for themselves, ‘WHAT THE HELL IS GOING ON?’ Have Fun and Enjoy!” Several files included military videos from the last several years that showed small ambiguous dots moving above the landscapes of Iraq, Syria and the United Arab Emirates. The white objects sometimes streaked across the screen in less than a second, while others slowly glided through the air or were followed by the camera.



Other documents included written reports from US military service members who were surveilling locations in the Middle East. One report described an object “shaped as a bouncy ball” and travelling 777 kilometres an hour consistently for at least seven minutes over Syria in 2023. The object was later determined to be benign. The Trump administration has previously released classified documents relating to the assassination of former president John F. Kennedy and civil rights activist Martin Luther King, but they revealed little information that was not already known. with AP Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Get papped with your mum by one of Australia’s hottest photographers on Mother’s Day
World.content:
CultureArt & designPhotography Get papped with your mum by one of Australia’s hottest photographers on Mother’s Day Kerrie O'Brien May 9, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Atong Atem’s striking photographs reflect identity, family, history and politics. She often uses herself as a canvas, painting her face, and the images she creates are often a riot of colour, playful and almost always joyous. On Sunday afternoon, in a pop-up event designed for Mother’s Day, Melburnians will have a chance to get a portrait shot by Atem – with their mum. Photographer Atong Atem with her baby. Ruby Alexander That said, the 35-year-old mother of two says her definition of mother for the pop-up is deliberately loose. To her mind, there are plenty of places where people can celebrate their mum in “that traditional flowers-and-chocolates way”.



Atong Atem’s Maria of Mars (2022). Courtesy of the NGV “I want just one little space in the world where it’s not about that ... Not everybody has the same relationship to Mother’s Day or mothers and family in general,” she says. “My mental image is that it’ll be everything from a mum bringing in their newborn baby and taking a photo with them, to somebody who doesn’t even like their mum ... and wants to take a photo that their mum would hate.” She also welcomes people who’ve lost mothers or lost mother figures, encouraging them to bring in a photo and have “a beautiful portrait taken as they hold a photo, or that person’s favourite dress or hat, or something symbolic and personal”. People are invited to sit for a 10-minute portrait session and can take a signed print home for $50. The main response thus far, she says, has been from people who aren’t planning to have a literal photograph taken with their mother.



Initially, Atem assumed it would just be her immediate circle of people interested but already there’s been a huge response. Entertainment will be provided by her eight-year-old nephew, who is a musician. Visitors are encouraged to BYO garments or hats that might need freshening up, as there will be an embroidery service on site; a number of volunteers will be on hand to help. Atong Atem with her work at ‘PHOTO 2022’. Luis Enrique Ascui Raised on the Central Coast in New South Wales, Atem is now based in Melbourne. After escaping the second civil war in her parents’ homeland of South Sudan, the family spent time in Kakuma refugee camp in north-west Kenya before arriving in Australia when she was six years old. Gallerist Andy Dinan of MARS Gallery recalls taking Atem’s work to Sydney Contemporary in 2019 and selling just one work; she cried on the plane on the way home. “Nine years on I’m laughing at how upset I was,” Dinan says.



Atem’s work has since been shown around the world, including at London’s Tate Modern, and is currently on display in Shanghai and Amsterdam. “[Atem’s work] is an examination of her displacement and also you can see her love of painting,” Dinan says. “She actually majored in painting and then went into photography, but you can see in her use of colour, how much she loves it. Atem’s “What we are given” (2024) was commissioned by the National Maritime Museum, Amsterdam. Atong Atem “She loves to photograph and is always working. She’s a delight to work with and her sense of community is second to none.” Dinan will take Atem’s new work to Sydney Contemporary in September and MARS will host a show in November.



In October, the National Gallery of Victoria will host a major survey show called Passage: The Art of Atong Atem. A world premiere, the exhibition will survey the past decade of her career, featuring more than 65 works. Related Article Literature How Shaun Tan’s book with no storyline inspired so many tattoos NGV director Tony Ellwood describes Atem as one of the most exciting artists of her generation, “redefining what it means to be Australian in contemporary life and culture”. “Her work aligns with the broader traditions of African studio photography, feminist aesthetics and diasporic storytelling. Yet, she has crafted a style and perspective that are uniquely her own, earning her recognition worldwide.” Atong Atem’s pop-up studio is at 99 Harding St, Coburg, from 1pm-5pm on Sunday, May 10.

World.title: Teals exploit donations gap in campaign to unseat Jess Wilson
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsVictoriaVictorian election Teals exploit donations gap in campaign to unseat Jess Wilson Chip Le Grand May 9, 2026 — 5:50am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Opposition Leader Jess Wilson will face a cashed-up independent challenger in her marginal seat of Kew for the first time after the funder of the teal movement, Climate 200, exploited a temporary gap in Victoria’s donation laws. Climate 200 co-convenor Simon Holmes à Court revealed to this masthead his organisation had tipped $40,000 into the campaign of independent candidate Sophie Torney, who is seeking to topple Wilson, and made a matching donation to Shima Ibuki, an independent running against former Liberal leader John Pesutto in Hawthorn. Opposition Leader Jess Wilson is facing a cashed-up challenger in her marginal seat of Kew. Luis Enrique Ascui The donations would have been illegal – and punishable by up to 10 years in jail – had they been made before April 15, when the High Court struck out Victoria’s campaign finance laws as unconstitutional. Under the previous regime, the maximum that any individual or organisation could donate to a candidate was $4970. There are currently no limits on the size of private donations to political candidates in Victoria, or any requirement for those donations to be disclosed.



The size of the Climate 200 contribution, which Holmes à Court said would be used to get the independent campaigns “off the ground” ahead of the November 28 election, will renew the urgency within the government and opposition to restore campaign finance rules. Related Article Updated

Victorian election Victorian election exposed after High Court strikes out campaign finance laws The Allan government had hoped to introduce legislation as early as Tuesday, when parliament next resumes, but is struggling to design a new framework that will satisfy its own caucus, win sufficient support within the parliament and withstand any further High Court challenge. Holmes à Court, who supported the successful High Court case of former independent candidates Paul Hopper and Melissa Lowe, defended Climate 200’s decision to make use of the regulatory vacuum. “Victorian taxpayers are funding almost the entire campaigns of their opponents, giving the majors a massive head start,” he said. “If we want remotely fair elections, we need to make sure challengers have adequate support to get off the ground.



“With just 202 days to the election, candidates can’t be expected to sit around and wonder how the state will clean up its mess.” He said he did not personally contribute to the donations. Centre for Public Integrity executive director Catherine Williams said Climate 200’s move underscored the need for the government to move quickly to restore transparency to the flow of campaign money. The Centre for Public Integrity is pushing for a restoration of disclosure requirements and public funding arrangements as an immediate step and the establishment of a more considered process after the election to develop a replacement campaign finance regime. “We anticipated that the period when Victoria lacked donations regulation was going to see an increase in the flow of money into campaigns,” Williams said. “That is the reason we want the government to at least restore transparency, urgently.



“What we ultimately want is for the parliament to put in place a comprehensive process to run post-election so this and other complex political finance regulation issues can be dealt with properly.” Premier Jacinta Allan has promised to backdate any changes to the Electoral Act to the day of the High Court decision. The influx of substantial donations into the teal campaigns in Kew and Hawthorn will reshape the contests in two of the Liberal Party’s vulnerable inner-city seats and invite further scrutiny of how Climate 200 funds community independents. Independent candidate Sophie Torney is running against Jess Wilson in the seat of Kew. Chris Hopkins Although Climate 200 is backed by high-worth individuals such as Holmes à Court, it says its electoral war chest is crowdfunding built from modest donations by more than 30,000 supporters.



It published an  in The Age on Saturday warning that this funding model, which it says involves average donations of just $33, would again be outlawed under the legislative fix being contemplated by the major parties. Holmes à Court has separately built an online portal titled “wall of advantage” which illustrates publicly funded benefits not available to independent challengers which incumbent MPs representing the major parties received to pay for political activities under the previous laws. He calculates that even in circumstances where a challenger is able to raise $250,000 in donations, they start more than $2 million behind a Labor or Coalition MP. Climate 200 founder Simon Holmes à Court. Oscar Colman David Feeney, a former Labor senator who recommended changes to Victoria’s campaign finance laws in a 2024 report, last week described the current vacuum as a regulatory catastrophe.



“The implications, unless a new system is established very, very swiftly, is that our November election becomes a billionaires’ picnic,” he told the Socially Democratic podcast. “What it means, in practical terms in November, is that teal independents, One Nation candidates – unless something changes – now have access to rivers of gold flowing into this state and into their political coffers.” Liberal MP David Davis went further. “It is hypocritical of the teals and Climate 200 to complain about donations when they are the first to make them,” he said. At the 2022 state election, independent candidates ran in Kew and Hawthorn but were kept campaign-poor by Victoria’s tight donation laws. Torney picked up 21 per cent of the vote in Kew, which Wilson holds by a margin of 4 per cent. Torney said the Climate 200 donation would get her 2026 campaign off the starting blocks.



“In Victoria, the major parties start every campaign with five to 10 times the resources of an independent and most of that gap is built from public money the major parties have funnelled to themselves,” she said. “That isn’t a fair contest.” The Victorian Trades Hall Council is also targeting the Liberal leader in her own seat, with a prominent billboard drawing attention to her party’s intention to preference One Nation candidates above Labor. Wilson says no decision has been made. Ibuki said the donation would make a material difference to her campaign in Hawthorn. “The High Court struck down the Victorian campaign finance laws for good reason, as the system rewarded the major parties and incumbents while putting huge barriers up against new independent candidate,” she said.



The High Court ruling centred on a carve-out under the old laws through which the major parties were able to receive unlimited campaign donations from legacy investment funds. The court found the arrangement, which was not available to smaller parties, new entrants or independents, was unfair and unconstitutional. The government, Liberal Party and Greens have agreed in backroom negotiations to reintroduce a cap on donations. There is no consensus on where the cap should be set, how much public funding there should be for political campaigns, and how to treat the legacy investment funds. World.title: The four-time Oscar winner who is a champion of cinemas, sex workers and Australian coffee
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The 2025 Academy Awards could not have gone better. After winning the top prize at the Cannes Film Festival, the wild romance Anora cleaned up at the Oscars, with Sean Baker winning four times – for best picture, director, original screenplay and editing. ‘Before I was really immersed in global cinema I was ready to make the next Die Hard, the next Robocop’: Sean Baker. Vivid Sydney Only Walt Disney had done that before at a single Oscars, for producing four different films. Baker did it with one: a wild contemporary tale shot for just $US6 million, for which little-known Mikey Madison won best actress for playing a New York lap dancer swept into a freewheeling romance with a young Russian. Related Article Good Weekend Forty years on, Paul Hogan’s Crocodile Dundee is still our biggest film. Here’s why it could have been a disaster On stage at the Oscars he talked about three of his passions: the vital importance of films screening in cinemas, respect for the sex worker community, and why independent filmmaking – outside the commercial imperatives of Hollywood studios – matters. Baker, a youthful-looking 55-year-old, works with distributors who value film as art, led by A24 and Neon. The subjects of his heartfelt films have been marginalised Americans, including sex workers, strippers and porn stars struggling to make a living in Starlet (2012), Tangerine (2015), The Florida Project (2017) and Red Rocket (2021). Since Anora, Baker has worked with long-time collaborator Shih-Ching Tsou on the Netflix film Left-Handed Girl (2025), set in a Taiwanese night market, and has directed a short for a fashion house, Sandiwara (2026), starring Michelle Yeoh and set in a Malaysian night market. He plans to shoot Ti Amo!, which is inspired by the Italian sex comedies of the 1960s and ’70s, this year.



Can we start, Sean, by talking about what that night at the Oscars was like for you? Incredible. It took me almost a year to process it: just the intense gratitude I had for everybody involved. It was a passion project for everybody, from the actors to the PAs. It was just a great celebration. It also meant I was able to get certain messages out during my speeches. The one that meant a lot to me was talking about the survival of movie theatres. Has all that success changed you as a filmmaker? I hope not. I try to check myself regularly. I’m going to stay in this independent space and perhaps get bigger budgets and get all of us paid a bit better. But I think what people like about my films is the DIY aspect of them. The indie/alt vibe that they bring. This success has allowed me to continue to do that. ‘The night before I went to that library I wanted to be a construction worker. The next morning I was telling my mum I wanted to make movies’: Sean Baker with his four Oscars for Anora. Getty Images Chloe Zhao made a Marvel movie, Eternals (2021), after her best picture-winning Nomadland (2020). Did you get offers to make a superhero film after Anora?



I didn’t, simply because I think I was so outspoken about the fact that I wasn’t interested. Chloe’s a good friend and I had a conversation with her about it. I’m like, “I haven’t gotten any calls”, and she goes, “I’ve heard directly from people at the studios that they would love to work with you if you want to but you’ve made it clear you don’t”. I grew up on very mainstream popcorn cinema. Until my freshman year at NYU, before I was really immersed in global cinema, I was ready to make the next Die Hard, the next Robocop. I may, perhaps down the line, want to figure out how to do that. But right now I have a fan base that is looking for a particular type of thing from me and I’m all up for delivering that. Why is the survival of cinemas so important to you? We’re losing theatres almost by the day. It’s tragic. COVID really hurt things because people forgot how great it is to see a movie with an audience. The advent of streaming made people get used to watching movies at home. And the reduction of theatrical windows no longer makes the theatrical experience special. If there’s a three-month-or-longer window I don’t see an issue with that. It will hopefully retrain the audience to say, “if I want to see a first-run movie I have to actually go to a theatre”. It’s how most filmmakers I know want their films to be seen – watching them with an audience where there are no distractions. There’s some hope because Gen Z [born between 1997 and 2012] is actually the biggest movie-going audience right now. How do you feel seeing someone watching a film on their phone? I’m like, ‘OK, you’re missing out’. It reduces the film to content and that’s pretty sad.



You once said that The Florida Project was the last film of your “sex worker trilogy”. Then you made two more with Red Rocket and Anora. What’s the appeal of characters who work in sex industry? I’d done so much research in that world and become friends with sex workers, who were consultants on these films, so [I knew] there were more stories to be told. After Florida Project we were going in a different direction. We had a film that we were developing that COVID killed overnight. That’s why we did a pivot to Red Rocket, which was an older idea on the back burner. It was exploring yet another world of sex work that just led naturally to Anora. I can tell you this, though: the next film does not contain sex work. Contains sex but not sex work. Mark Eydelshteyn and Mikey Madison in Anora. AP How early did you want to become a filmmaker? My mother brought me to the local library when I was five years old and they were showing clips from Universal monster films. It was the burning windmill sequence of James Whale’s 1931 Frankenstein that really did it for me. I’ve talked to Guillermo [del Toro, whose latest film is Frankenstein] about this. That was the film that also made him fall in love with the movies. The night before I went to that library I wanted to be a construction worker. The next morning I was telling my mum I wanted to make movies.



Your mother was a teacher and your father was a patent attorney, and you’ve described them as “wonderful people, very ethical”. Is that where your empathy for marginalised people comes from? I think so. The pursuit of empathy – to try to understand the plight of others – was something they helped forge. I went to a prep school in New Jersey, Gill St Bernard’s, that was very liberal. We were doing things in the ’80s that I don’t think public schools were doing – exploring the Iran-Contra affair and meeting with undocumented immigrants from El Salvador escaping persecution. So perhaps it also came from there. Sean Baker embraces Anora star Mikey Madison after one of his Oscar wins last year. Chris Pizzello/Invision/AP Has it become harder to tell stories about an American underclass in the “end wokeness” Trump era? I don’t think so. Our class divide is still as strong as ever. That’s what I’m exploring more – the class divide. If I look back at my films, that’s what I see. And also underground economies. I don’t think the Trump administration has changed that. Do you see yourself as an activist as much as a filmmaker? Interesting. With activism there has to be an overt stance. Not that I don’t have them but I don’t think it’s my job to preach to audiences. My job is to ask questions and to spark conversation and debate.

World.title: Labor announces $40 million boost to address firearms registry failings
World.content:
The government will inject nearly $40 million into the state’s firearm registry in a bid to overhaul the troubled system and increase community safety following the Bondi shooting terror attack in December last year.

On Saturday, police minister Yasmin Catley announced the $39.3 million investment, which will also fund additional staff and system upgrades, to accompany a suite of tighter restrictions on gun owners.

Police Minister Yasmin Catley, who had described the NSW Firearms Registry as a “shambles”, and Premier Chris Minns. Dominic Lorrimer

The new restrictions reduce the licence period from five years to two, strengthen checks on people seeking to own firearms and cap the number of firearms a person can own. A comprehensive audit of all existing firearm licences will also be undertaken.

It follows a report in this masthead revealing that, during a meeting at police headquarters on December 8, 2020, psychologist and gun club official Daniel Gregg warned officials from the NSW Police Firearms Registry that far too little was being done to encourage club members to spot and report any signs of extremism among their fellow shooters.
